summary: A working document describing the Decode-Encode Language (DEL), a machine-independent language for two network tasks: taking input from interactive consoles and packing it into messages, and unpacking incoming messages to build display information for a user. It was written at SRI and invited comments as the language evolved.

plainLanguage.summary: DEL was proposed as a machine-independent language for translating interactive input and display information across the ARPA network. This working document outlines how programs written in DEL could encode user input and decode responses.

subtitle: A working paper on a language for interactive communication across the ARPA network.

tldr.problem: Interactive programs had to accept input from different consoles, provide local feedback, and exchange information with remote hosts.
tldr.mechanism: The Decode-Encode Language (DEL) describes programs that translate console input into network messages and incoming messages into display information.
tldr.outcome: The RFC calls itself a working document for the evolution of DEL and invites comments; it is not presented as a final standard.

today: RFC 5 is listed with status Unknown. Its text describes it as a working document for the evolution of DEL and does not state a later outcome.

sections.title: The Decode-Encode Language
sections.content:
Jeff Rulifson's Decode-Encode Language (DEL) is tailored to two network tasks: accepting input codes from interactive consoles and packing information into message packets, and receiving packets, unpacking them, and building display information.

The document grew from discussions about running interactive programs across the network. It describes DEL as a working document for the language's continued evolution.
sections.plainLanguage: DEL was intended to handle input from an interactive console and information returned from a remote computer. This RFC presents a working description, not a completed standard.

sections.title: Network Standard Translators
sections.content:
The Network Standard Translator (NST) library works with code compiled at a user site from symbolic DEL programs received from a server host. In a simple use, a DEL program builds and sends messages.

In a more involved use, it echoes and translates console characters, packs them into messages, and displays messages received from the server. For display-oriented systems, the user-host program can provide immediate feedback and send messages when appropriate input occurs.
sections.plainLanguage: A host could send a DEL program to the user's computer, where it would be compiled for that machine. The program could translate console input and display the server's responses.

sections.title: A Common Device Representation
sections.content:
To reduce the number of translators needed, the RFC proposes a universal hardware representation for interactive devices. For example, it describes a display as a square with coordinates ranging from -1 to 1 on each axis.

This lets a point be represented without depending on the number or density of raster points on a particular display. The document says the representation is explained with the formal DEL description.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal gives devices a shared description so programs need fewer host-specific translations. A display point can be described with normalized coordinates rather than the display's pixel layout.

sections.title: The DEL Language Description
sections.content:
The paper includes syntax for declarations, procedures, functions, co-routines, arithmetic, control flow, tree manipulation, message construction, and display buffers. It describes message operations such as starting, appending to, and sending a message.

The paper also contains open questions and sample fragments. It presents this language description as material for continued discussion and development.
sections.plainLanguage: The document sketches language features for processing input, building messages, and describing displays. It remains a working document with questions left open.
